reason: Perceptual comparison covers sets so unequal that number and size agree. The test pits number against size and spread, so a perceptual judgment is exactly what the node must override and cannot supply the meaning. It is a developmental precursor for the word 'more', not a requirement.
why: The learner must already judge which of two very unequal sets has more before the meaning of 'more' can be tied to number rather than size.

reason: The fence test asks whether a boundary has a gap; a child who cannot yet recognize triangles or squares as such can still see that a fence is open. The shapes in the figures are incidental to the idea of closure.
why: The statement contrasts a complete triangle or square with a gapped figure, so the learner must already see the intended shape.

reason: Wrong as a required edge - neither the concept nor the test of a closed boundary needs the words inside and outside.
why: Inside and outside (the sheep cannot get out) is the idea the fence test uses; it may need position words such as inside and outside. Weak candidate, depends on the node's content.

reason: Wrong as a required edge - matching identical shapes may help, but direct labeling and classification are credible routes to selecting a shape by its name.
why: Picking the named shape from a set means the child already sees which shapes are the same shape and which are different.

reason: Claude (C13, D21): in Common Core negatives are first met in 6.NS.C.5, through opposite quantities in context, and this node is one of those contexts; the sign convention is introduced here, so no prior negative-number meaning is needed (Daniel: a decrease context can itself introduce negatives).
why: The statement writes a decrease with a negative number, so the learner must already know a negative number as the opposite of a positive amount.

reason: Wrong as a required edge - signed change can be introduced from context without subtraction.
why: The idea of a decrease as an amount removed may need subtraction; weak candidate, depends on how the node treats 'decrease'.
